events.credibility_reason: Content unread; ProofWiki excerpt reports mistakes in the source.
Author calls results preliminary and search-based; no proof that the repeating pattern holds for all n; base-20 seed not transcribed.
Abstract only, from a search excerpt; the 'generalised existence proof' it mentions is not given anywhere in the record.

Lychrel is redefined as a palindrome-reaching probability below (1/10)^330, which cannot show that any orbit never reaches a palindrome, and the paper says its result 'remains probabilistic'; low-review SCIRP venue; no expert uptake or citation in about 26 months on a problem whose resolution would be news; Wikipedia, as updated in 2026, still calls the question open; internal inconsistency in the list of proven bases.

why: The statement is the Wikipedia list's entry for Lychrel numbers, which are defined in base 10 by default; the list treats the question as open even though base-2 examples were known since 1969. So I read the base-2 and other-base results (Brousseau, Johns-Wiegold, Kröber, Seal) as answers to an analogue (variant), not as a whole answer to the base-unqualified wording. The 196 computations are finite instances. Kuitché's paper is the close call. Its existence 'proof' replaces 'never reaches a palindrome' with a probability threshold, which changes the question (variant). Even if it were read as a claim to the whole question, its signals together put it at not_credible: a self-described probabilistic method that cannot reach the deterministic claim, a weak venue, no uptake, and later sources still calling the problem open. Either reading sets it aside. The Mahiddini abstract has only a year-2024 date, so it cannot be placed; it reports numerics and mentions a proof without giving it, so its scope is none. No AI was involved in any event.
doubts: If the bullet is read literally without a base, the 1969 base-2 seed 10110 (checkable by induction) would answer it in full before the snapshot, giving open_stale instead of open. I chose the base-10 reading because the Wikipedia article's own box asks about base 10. Attribution of the base-2 result (Brousseau, Sprague or Brockhaus) is unresolved. The Kuitché PDF body was not read.
